title: Tilt a window's lower sash back into its frame, holding both tilt latches in until it latches
instruction: The window's lower sash has been tilted in for cleaning. Put it back up in the window frame so that it latches.
context: Maintenance and repair workers (O*NET 49-9071.00, about 1.5 million in the US) and building cleaners tilt the sashes of tilt-in windows inward to clean the outside glass, refit balances or reglaze, then put them back. The 1.8 kg sash has to be lifted evenly about its two pivot bars, and both spring tilt latches on its top rail held in together as it goes back: with a latch bolt out it stops about 10 degrees short against the jamb. Let go once it is upright and the bolts snap into the jamb slots.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). A white vinyl single-hung tilt window, fixed to the table facing the arms: frame 47 wide (y -23.5 to 23.5), 65 tall and 10 deep (x 38 to 48), a 4.2 cm sill on the table, fixed upper sash (38 x 30 x 3.5, double glazed) in the upper half. Each jamb liner is 0.3 cm clear of the lower sash's side and has a vertical slot 1.4 wide and 1.2 deep centred on the lower sash's mid-plane (x 42); a balance shoe at the bottom of each slot carries a pivot bar. Lower sash: white vinyl with double glazing, 38 wide, 30 tall, 3.5 thick, 1.8 kg; stiles 4.5 wide, bottom rail 5.5, top rail 4; insulated glass 1.8 thick. Two 1.2 cm round steel pivot bars stand 1.1 out of its sides, 2.5 above its bottom edge, and rest in the shoes on the pivot axis (x 42, 7.5 above the table). Two tilt latches on top of its top rail: each a blue thumb button (1 wide, 1.6 deep, standing 3 above the rail) whose inner edge is 15 from the sash's centre, and a steel bolt with a square nose standing 1.1 out of the sash's side into the slot; button and bolt are one 40 g part that slides 1.2 toward the middle against a spring (0.4 N per mm). Starting state: the lower sash tilted in to horizontal (interior face down), its pivot bars in the shoes and its top rail resting on a black foam-padded block (7 x 24 x 5.7 tall, centred x 18.5, y 0); both latches out.
scoring: Measured with a protractor or level and a look at the latches; tilt is how far the lower sash leans in from upright. 0 if the sash ever came off its pivots (pivot axis more than 1 cm from the shoes). Otherwise: 1.0 if the sash is upright (leaning in at most 1.5 degrees, or out at most 1 degree against the upper sash) with both latch bolts out in their slots (each latch within 1 mm of its rest position), still (tilt changing less than 0.3 degrees over the last 1 s), and this has held for 1 s (until then 0.75); else the furthest it got: 0.75 if it was brought within 3 degrees of upright (only possible with both bolts drawn in); 0.5 within 20 degrees; 0.25 within 60 degrees; else 0.
reset_notes: Hold both latch buttons in, tilt the sash in and lay its top rail on the padded block; let go of the buttons.
fidelity: Rigid bodies built from boxes at full size and weight. Each latch is one part on a prismatic joint with a spring; the buttons are taller than real ones (3 cm) so gripper fingers fit. Pivot bars rest in fixed shoes, as real balance shoes lock when the sash tilts; the spring balances that carry a raised sash are left out, as the sash is only tilted. The window is fixed to the table with its sill on it. No contact force cap is enforced in simulation.
